transcript.text: Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining this medication safety huddle. As you know, the hospital introduced the intravenous anticoagulant protocol on Monday for adult inpatients. The medication is currently stocked in automated dispensing cabinets and ordered through the electronic medication record. Before I sign off on the afternoon decision to use this protocol on the night shift, I need to hear from each of you regarding any operational findings. I'd like to go through each area systematically. Could pharmacy, laboratory medicine, nursing education, and clinical information technology each report any findings or concerns you've identified? I'll wait to hear from all of you before making my final decision on the protocol and any required safeguards.
transcript.speaker: A1

transcript.text: I need to report a significant safety concern from pharmacy. Since Monday, I've verified three selection errors involving the 1 mg/mL and 2 mg/mL anticoagulant concentrations. Given the risk of concentration mix-ups at the bedside, I'd recommend that pharmacy remove the bedside stock from the automated dispensing cabinets and instead supply only pharmacy-prepared 1 mg/mL syringes during a temporary hold. This would eliminate the selection risk while still allowing the protocol to be used on the night shift.
transcript.speaker: A2

transcript.text: From laboratory medicine, I need to report an important operational finding. The anti-Xa analyzer is unavailable for calibration until Friday at 17:00. During this period, the laboratory's approved replacement for monitoring patients on this anticoagulant protocol is an aPTT test every six hours. This monitoring schedule needs to be communicated to nursing and clinical IT so that orders and lab draws are aligned accordingly.
transcript.speaker: A3

transcript.text: From nursing education, I need to report an urgent staffing concern. My competency roster shows that 18 nurses scheduled for tonight have not completed the new anticoagulant administration module. Each of these nurses must receive charge-nurse sign-off before administering the medication. This is a significant safeguard that needs to be in place before the protocol is used on the night shift.

transcript.text: From clinical information technology, I can report that I've confirmed a high-priority electronic medication-record alert can be deployed at 16:00 today. This alert will warn clinicians about concentration selection and require acknowledgment before the order can be released. This directly addresses the selection errors Leah identified and serves as an additional layer of safety alongside any other safeguards we implement for the night shift.
